Granular mobility data for Indian cities is either unavailable or personal
enough that releasing it is not an option. Synthetic data is a way through:
reproduce the statistical structure of the real thing without reproducing
anyone in it, and get a sandbox for scenarios that no observed dataset can
answer.

## Three scripts

**Population.** Builds a synthetic population for Bandra carrying the
demographic and socio-economic structure of the ward, from points of interest
and a boundary shapefile.

**Mobility.** Simulates trips probabilistically against land use, transit
availability and behavioural assumptions; trip points are generated through a
kernel density surface rather than uniformly, so origins concentrate where
activity concentrates.

**Evaluation.** Calibrates the output by comparing aggregate metrics with the
limited real data that is available, then models demand per hexagon with a
random forest and tests the result for spatial structure with local Moran's I.

![Local Moran's I clusters of predicted demand across the hexagon grid. Whether
the synthetic surface clusters at all, and where, is the check on whether the
generator reproduced spatial structure or only marginal
distributions](../images/som787-morans.png)

## Limitations

Synthetic data inherits its assumptions and hides them well. The population is
representative in aggregate and fictitious individually, so results hold at the
scale of the calibration and not below it. The calibration itself is only as
good as the sparse observations it is fitted against, which is the same data
scarcity the method was built to work around.
